title: Comparing Fractions
subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Understand the meaning of numerator and denominator as equal parts of a whole.
Compare fractions with equal numerators, equal denominators, or different denominators accurately.
Recognize that larger denominators mean more partitions and therefore smaller individual unit parts when wholes are identical.
Understand and construct equivalent fractions via proportional scaling rather than addition.

concepts.title: Understanding Fractions
learning_objectives: Identify the numerator as the count of selected parts.
Identify the denominator as the total number of equal parts dividing the whole.
Understand that parts of the whole must be equal in size.
Interpret a fraction as a specific numerical quantity.
concepts.verified_explanation: A fraction represents part of a whole divided into equal-sized parts. The bottom number, the denominator, tells us how many equal parts the whole is partitioned into. The top number, the numerator, counts how many of those equal parts are being considered.
concepts.intuitive_analogy: Imagine sharing a birthday cake. The denominator is the total number of identical slices cut from the whole cake. The numerator is how many slices you put on your plate.

steps: Start with one whole unit (e.g. one circular pizza or rectangular strip).
Divide the unit into 4 equal-sized pieces (denominator is 4).
Take or shade 3 of those pieces (numerator is 3).
3/4 represents the quantity of 3 one-fourth parts.

common_mistakes: Assuming pieces do not need to be equal in size.
concepts.source_reference: National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) Numbers and Operations Standard: Fractions

concepts.title: Comparing Fractions
learning_objectives: Compare fractions with equal numerators (e.g. 2/5 vs 2/3).
Compare fractions with equal denominators (e.g. 3/8 vs 5/8).
Compare fractions using equivalent fractions or benchmark comparisons (e.g. 1/2).
Understand why a larger denominator produces smaller unit pieces for the same whole.
concepts.verified_explanation: When comparing fractions of the same whole: If denominators are equal, more parts (greater numerator) means a greater fraction. If numerators are equal, dividing into fewer parts produces larger individual parts (so smaller denominator means greater fraction). If both differ, find a common denominator or compare against benchmark 1/2.
concepts.intuitive_analogy: If you split a single pizza among 3 friends, each person gets a much larger slice than if you split the same pizza among 5 friends! So 1/3 slice is bigger than 1/5 slice, and 2/3 of a pizza is greater than 2/5.

steps: Both fractions have the same numerator: 2 parts.
Dividing a whole into 3 equal pieces makes each piece (1/3) bigger than dividing into 5 pieces (1/5).
Therefore, 2 pieces of size 1/3 (2/3) must be larger than 2 pieces of size 1/5 (2/5).
Alternatively, common denominator is 15: 2/5 = 6/15, and 2/3 = 10/15. Since 10/15 > 6/15, 2/3 is larger.

common_mistakes: Reversed denominator rule: assuming a bigger denominator always makes a bigger number.
concepts.source_reference: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.4.NF.A.2)

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions
learning_objectives: Understand that equivalent fractions represent the exact same quantity of a whole.
Generate equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer.
Recognize that adding the same number to numerator and denominator changes the value.
concepts.verified_explanation: Equivalent fractions have different numbers but equal value. Multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number is multiplying the fraction by 1 (e.g. 2/2 = 1), preserving its magnitude. Adding a number to both changes the ratio and alters the value.
concepts.intuitive_analogy: Cutting each slice of a pizza in half doubles the number of slices you have (numerator) and also doubles the total number of slices in the whole pizza (denominator). You have more slices, but the same amount of pizza!

steps: Since 2/2 = 1, multiplying 1/2 by 2/2 does not change the quantity.
Both represent exactly half of the whole.

common_mistakes: Believing that adding 1 to numerator and denominator preserves equivalence (e.g. 1/2 != 2/3).
Multiplying only the numerator or only the denominator.
concepts.source_reference: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.4.NF.A.1)
